title: What load-balancing algorithms exist (round robin, least connections, least response time, IP hash / sticky sessions, weighted, consistent hashing), and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What load-balancing algorithms exist, and when do you use each?
keyPoints: Round robin cycles requests in order across equal instances, simple but load-blind.
Least connections sends each request to the instance with the fewest active connections, adapting to variable request durations.
Least response time routes toward the instance with the lowest recent latency, best for heterogeneous instances.
IP hash and sticky sessions pin a client to one instance, needed only when the instance holds client-specific local state.
Weighted variants assign more traffic to more powerful instances, useful for canary deployments and heterogeneous fleets.
Consistent hashing maps instances and keys onto a hash ring so adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys.
Every algorithm must be paired with health checks so dead instances leave rotation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Pick round robin for uniform equal instances, least connections for variable request lengths, least response time for uneven instances, sticky or IP hash when local state ties a client to an instance, weighted for unequal capacity, and consistent hashing when instances come and go and you must minimize remapping.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Round Robin** – cycles through instances in order, ideal for uniform requests and equal instances, but ignores actual load.
- **Least Connections** – sends each request to the instance with the fewest active connections, adapting when request durations vary.
- **Least Response Time** – picks the instance with the lowest observed latency, best when instances differ in speed.
- **IP Hash / Sticky Sessions** – pins a client to a consistent instance, needed when the instance holds client-specific local state.
- **Weighted** – assigns more traffic to more powerful instances, used for heterogeneous fleets and canary rollouts.
- **Consistent Hashing** – maps instances and keys onto a hash ring so adding or removing an instance remaps only a small fraction of keys, essential for distributed caches.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the floor manager at National Bank of India assigning arriving customers to teller windows. Round robin is "next customer to the next window in order." Least connections is "send the next customer to the window with the shortest queue right now." IP hash is "Mr. Rajesh always goes to window three because that teller holds his half-finished paperwork." Consistent hashing is a smart seating chart where opening or closing one window only reshuffles a few customers instead of the whole hall.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Consistent Hashing Ring
  ────────────────────────

                0
           ┌────┴────┐
          /           \
    cache-3            cache-1
        │               │
        │   hash ring   │
        │               │
    cache-2            cache-4
          \           /
           └────┬────┘
               512

  Adding cache-4 remaps only keys in its arc (~25%).
  Removing cache-2 remaps only its keys to cache-3.
  Virtual nodes (100 per instance) smooth the distribution.


  Algorithm Decision Tree
  ───────────────────────

  Is it a cache or sharded store? ──Yes──► Consistent Hashing
       │
       No
       │
  Does the instance hold client state? ──Yes──► IP Hash / Sticky
       │                                        (but externalize state!)
       No
       │
  Are instances unequal in capacity? ──Yes──► Weighted Round Robin
       │
       No
       │
  Do request durations vary widely? ──Yes──► Least Connections
       │
       No
       │
  ► Round Robin (simplest default)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Load-balancing algorithms decide which backend instance serves each request, and the right choice follows the workload. Round robin simply cycles through instances in order and is fair when requests are uniform and instances are equal, but it is load-blind. Least connections sends each request to the instance with the fewest active connections, which adapts naturally when request durations vary. Least response time routes toward the fastest instance, best for heterogeneous fleets.

IP hash and sticky sessions pin a client to a consistent instance, but stickiness is a smell: it undermines even distribution and breaks on instance death, so the better fix is to externalize state. Weighted variants assign more traffic to more powerful instances, useful for canary deployments. Consistent hashing maps instances and keys onto a ring so adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys, which is essential for distributed caches and sharded stores.

Every algorithm must be paired with health checks so a dead instance leaves rotation immediately. The senior judgment is to match the algorithm to the workload: round robin for uniform requests, least connections as a sensible default, consistent hashing for caches and shards, and stickiness only as a temporary measure until state is externalized.

Remember one sentence: round robin for uniform equal instances, least connections for variable durations, consistent hashing for caches, and always pair with health checks.
